messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: rstan wish: graceful failures
parts:
Particularly when doing parallel calculations, failures cause problems
(I've also had failures because of insufficient RAM):

> sflist <- mclapply(1:3, function(i) stan(fit=rb, data=stanDat, iter=8000, chains=1,
+ seed=seed, chain_id=i, refresh=-1,
+ warmup=500, thin=4),
+ mc.cores=3)
Initialization failed after 100 attempts. Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

> a10 <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)
Error in sflist2stanfit(sflist) :
each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples

Wish #1: sflist2stanfit would combine all the valid runs. There may be
some subtleties in terms of the reported number of chains/iterations,
since using the original request isn't right.

Wish #2: make it easier to identify which objects have useable results.
My first thought was
> lapply(sflist, class)
[[1]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

[[2]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

[[3]]
[1] "stanfit"
attr(,"package")
[1] "rstan"

Nope, they all have the same class.

Reading the fine manual, I think the mode slot has the info I want.
> lapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode)
[[1]]
[1] 0

[[2]]
[1] 2

[[3]]
[1] 0

Wrapping that in an is.valid function (or some similar name) would be
helpful.

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan wish: graceful failures
parts:
Thanks for the suggestions.

There's an issue with maintaining the appropriate posteriors
if you just excise chains from the collection. On the other
hand, you bring up a good point about running out of RAM. Can
you just not include the bad runs in the list in the first place?

Initialization failure signals a problem with the model,
but one of those problems is numerical precision, which
isn't totally under the user's control. We're going to try
to clean that up in the future, but right now, for instance,
high-dimensional correlation matrices are causing numerical
issues.

- Bob

I'm not sure which list you are referring to, the first argument to
mclapply (1:3) or the sflist object.

What I did was just create a list with only good elements, and then
hand that to sflist2stanfit.

It sounds as if you are saying the result may not have the right
posterior distribution.

> Initialization failure signals a problem with the model,

> to clean that up in the future, but right now, for instance,
> high-dimensional correlation matrices are causing numerical
> issues.

At any rate, I need to look into the failure rather than use the
resulting truncated results. It doesn't look to me as if it should be
that easy to get values that cause calculation problems.

Ross

On 10/15/13 3:44 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Mon, Oct 14, 2013 at 04:24:01AM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Thanks for the suggestions.
>>
>> There's an issue with maintaining the appropriate posteriors
>> if you just excise chains from the collection. On the other
>> hand, you bring up a good point about running out of RAM. Can
>> you just not include the bad runs in the list in the first place?
>
> I'm not sure which list you are referring to, the first argument to
> mclapply (1:3) or the sflist object.
>
> What I did was just create a list with only good elements, and then
> hand that to sflist2stanfit.
>
> It sounds as if you are saying the result may not have the right
> posterior distribution.

Correct. You can't just drop chains and maintain the right
expectations. It might work in this case, though it's not
guaranteed. (For example, you can't drop chains that just
get stuck.) We need to do more research on this, both theoretical
and practical, before we come up with a fix.

>>
>> Initialization failure signals a problem with the model,
>> but one of those problems is numerical precision, which
>> isn't totally under the user's control. We're going to try
>> to clean that up in the future, but right now, for instance,
>> high-dimensional correlation matrices are causing numerical
>> issues.
>
> At any rate, I need to look into the failure rather than use the
> resulting truncated results. It doesn't look to me as if it should be
> that easy to get values that cause calculation problems.

The best I can suggest is print statements in the code wrapped
in conditionals for particular cases.

- Bob
